blocks.text: A machinist wants to know, without cutting a test bar, whether a shaft is soft annealed steel or a quenched and tempered one. A 3 mm dent from a 10 mm ball in 30 seconds can answer that, and the dent also predicts tensile strength within about 10 percent.

blocks.markdown: Hardness is the resistance of a surface to localised plastic deformation by an indenter. Because it needs only a small, almost non-destructive indent, it is widely used for quality control. Hardness correlates with strength because both depend on the stress needed to move dislocations in the material.

blocks.title: Brinell and Vickers hardness
blocks.text: Brinell: a hardened ball of diameter $D$ is pressed with force $F$ and the diameter $d$ of the permanent circular impression is measured; HB is load divided by the curved contact area. Vickers: a square diamond pyramid (136 degree apex angle) is pressed with force $F$ and the mean diagonal $d$ of the impression is measured. With $F$ in kgf and lengths in mm, both give numbers in kgf/mm$^2$.

blocks.caption: $F$ in kgf, $D$ and $d$ in mm; hardness in kgf/mm$^2$. For $F$ in newtons, divide by 9.807 first.

blocks.title: Brinell hardness of a steel
blocks.prompt: A steel is tested with a 10.0 mm ball at 3000 kgf, leaving an impression of diameter 4.0 mm. Find HB and estimate the tensile strength with $\mathrm{TS}\approx3.45\,\mathrm{HB}$ (MPa).

steps.text: Compute the depth term: $\sqrt{D^2-d^2}=\sqrt{100-16}=9.165$ mm, so $D-\sqrt{D^2-d^2}=0.835$ mm.

blocks.answer: HB $\approx229$ and the tensile strength is about 790 MPa.

Large indent, averages over grains; for softer metals; valid for $0.25D<d<0.5D$
Same scale from soft to hard; small indent for thin sections

Fast, direct reading; dimensionless scales such as HRC and HRB

blocks.title: Vickers hardness from a measured diagonal
blocks.prompt: A Vickers test with $F=30$ kgf gives a mean diagonal of 0.42 mm. Find HV and estimate the tensile strength, assuming $\mathrm{HV}\approx\mathrm{HB}$ at this hardness.

steps.text: Use the steel rule with HB approximated by HV.

blocks.answer: HV $\approx315$ and TS $\approx1090$ MPa, an approximate estimate only.

blocks.markdown:
**How metals are strengthened.** Plastic deformation in a crystal is by dislocation glide, so any obstacle to dislocation motion raises the yield strength. Three main mechanisms:

- *Grain refinement*: dislocations pile up at grain boundaries and cannot cross easily because adjacent grains have different slip-plane orientations. Smaller grains mean more boundary area. The Hall-Petch relation is $\sigma_y=\sigma_0+k_y\,d^{-1/2}$, where $d$ is the mean grain diameter and $\sigma_0$, $k_y$ are material constants.
- *Solid solution strengthening*: solute atoms of a different size distort the surrounding lattice, and the strain fields interact with dislocations, which must be pushed harder to pass.
- *Strain (work) hardening*: cold working multiplies dislocations, which tangle and block one another.

items: Grain refinement raises strength and also toughness, which is unusual.
Solid solution strengthening is stronger for larger size mismatch and higher solute content.
Strain hardening raises strength but lowers ductility, and can be reversed by annealing.
All three raise hardness as well as yield strength, so hardness testing can monitor them.

blocks.title: Approximate hardness-strength link
blocks.text: For steels, $\mathrm{TS}\ (\mathrm{MPa})\approx3.45\,\mathrm{HB}$. The relation is empirical; use it for screening, not for design allowables.

points: Brinell uses a ball and the impression diameter; Vickers uses a diamond pyramid and the diagonal; Rockwell uses the depth.
Grain refinement, solid solution and strain hardening all strengthen a metal by making dislocation motion harder.

questions.stem: Which hardness test determines the hardness number from the depth of penetration under a major load, read directly from a dial or display?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Rockwell takes the permanent depth increase after a minor and major load as the measure.
distractorRationale.b: Brinell measures the diameter of the impression left by a ball, using optical measurement.
distractorRationale.c: Vickers measures the diagonals of a square pyramidal impression optically.
distractorRationale.d: Only Rockwell uses the depth; Brinell and Vickers use the size of the residual impression.

questions.explanation: The Rockwell test applies a small minor load to seat the indenter, then a major load, and the hardness number is derived from the extra permanent depth. Brinell and Vickers instead optically measure the surface dimensions (diameter or diagonal) of the residual impression.

questions.stem: Reducing the grain size of a polycrystalline metal increases its yield strength, because grain boundaries obstruct the motion of dislocations.
questions.explanation: Dislocations cannot easily cross a grain boundary, because the slip planes in neighbouring grains have different orientations, so dislocations pile up at boundaries. Smaller grains mean more boundary area per unit volume, which raises the yield strength, described by the Hall-Petch relation.

questions.stem: A Brinell test uses a 10.0 mm diameter ball with a load of 3000 kgf and leaves an impression of diameter 4.5 mm. Calculate the Brinell hardness number HB (in kgf/mm$^2$), using $\mathrm{HB}=\dfrac{2F}{\pi D\left(D-\sqrt{D^2-d^2}\right)}$.
questions.explanation: The term $\sqrt{D^2-d^2}=\sqrt{100-20.25}=8.930$ mm, so $D-\sqrt{D^2-d^2}=1.070$ mm. Then $\mathrm{HB}=2(3000)/[\pi(10)(1.070)]=6000/33.6=178.5$. This is the number in kgf/mm$^2$, though by convention it is quoted without units.

questions.stem: A Vickers test uses a load $F=10$ kgf and gives a mean impression diagonal $d=0.25$ mm. Using $\mathrm{HV}=1.8544\,F/d^2$ (with $F$ in kgf and $d$ in mm), what is the Vickers hardness number?

distractorRationale.b: This divides $F$ by $d^2$ without the factor 1.8544.
distractorRationale.d: This uses $d=0.125$ mm, the half-diagonal, in the formula.

questions.explanation: The Vickers pyramid has an apex angle of 136 degrees, so the contact area is $d^2/(2\sin68^\circ)=d^2/1.8544$. The hardness is load divided by that area: $1.8544\times10/0.0625=297$.

questions.stem: A carbon steel has a measured Brinell hardness of 215 HB. Using the approximate relation $\mathrm{TS}\ (\mathrm{MPa})\approx3.45\times\mathrm{HB}$ for steels, estimate the tensile strength in MPa.
questions.explanation: Using $\mathrm{TS}\approx3.45\,\mathrm{HB}$: $3.45\times215=741.75\approx742$ MPa. This empirical relation holds for steels (not for all alloys) and is accurate to perhaps 10 percent.

questions.stem: Use the Hall-Petch relation $\sigma_y=\sigma_0+k_y\,d^{-1/2}$ with assumed values $\sigma_0=50$ MPa and $k_y=0.60$ MPa m$^{1/2}$. Calculate the yield strength of a metal with an average grain diameter of $25\ \mu$m, in MPa.
questions.explanation: With $d=25\times10^{-6}$ m, $d^{-1/2}=1/\sqrt{25\times10^{-6}}=200$ m$^{-1/2}$. Then $\sigma_y=50+0.60\times200=170$ MPa; for comparison, $d=100\ \mu$m would give 110 MPa, so a four-fold reduction in grain diameter raises the yield strength by 60 MPa.

questions.stem: A steel is found to have a tensile strength of 690 MPa. Using $\mathrm{TS}\approx3.45\,\mathrm{HB}$ (TS in MPa), what Brinell hardness would you expect?

distractorRationale.b: This multiplies 690 by 3.45 instead of dividing.
distractorRationale.c: This confuses the TS in MPa with the hardness number.
distractorRationale.d: This halves the value with no basis in the relation.

questions.explanation: The empirical rule for steels is $\mathrm{TS}=3.45\,\mathrm{HB}$ in MPa, so HB is TS divided by 3.45, which is $690/3.45=200$. The relation holds because both are measures of the flow stress needed to drive plastic deformation.

questions.stem: A bar of annealed copper is cold-rolled so its thickness is reduced by 30 percent. Which statement correctly describes the strengthening mechanism and its consequence?

options.text: Dislocation density rises and the dislocations tangle and block each other, so yield strength increases and ductility decreases
Dislocations are annihilated, so the metal becomes softer and more ductile
Grains become larger, so grain boundaries obstruct dislocations less
Solute atoms from the rolls dissolve in the copper

questions.correctOptionText: Dislocation density rises and the dislocations tangle and block each other, so yield strength increases and ductility decreases

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is strain hardening or work hardening.
distractorRationale.b: This describes recovery or annealing, not cold work.
distractorRationale.c: Cold work does not coarsen grains; it elongates them and raises the dislocation density.
distractorRationale.d: Rolling does not introduce solute; the strengthening is by dislocation interaction.

questions.explanation: Plastic deformation multiplies dislocations. These interact, tangle and create obstacles to each other's motion, so a higher stress is needed to keep deforming, and the remaining ductility is reduced.

questions.stem: Describe how each of grain refinement, solid solution strengthening and strain hardening impedes dislocation motion, and state one drawback or limit of each.
markingGuide: Grain refinement: boundaries are barriers because slip planes change orientation, so dislocations pile up; yield strength follows $d^{-1/2}$ (2 marks)
Solid solution: solute atoms distort the lattice and their strain fields interact with dislocations, requiring more stress to move them (2 marks)
Strain hardening: dislocation density increases and dislocations tangle and obstruct each other (2 marks)

Drawbacks: ductility falls with cold work (1 mark); grain refinement is limited by processing and by grain growth at high temperature (1 mark); solute raises strength but may reduce conductivity (1 mark)
questions.explanation: Each mechanism creates obstacles to dislocation glide: boundaries, solute strain fields or other dislocations. The common consequence is higher strength with lower ductility or other penalties.

questions.stem: A Brinell test on a steel with a 10.0 mm ball at 3000 kgf gives an impression of diameter 3.0 mm. Calculate HB, estimate the tensile strength from $\mathrm{TS}\approx3.45\,\mathrm{HB}$, and comment on whether the impression is within the usual validity limit of $0.25D<d<0.5D$.
markingGuide: $d=3.0$ mm lies between 2.5 mm and 5.0 mm, so the test is valid (1 mark)
States that the TS relation is an approximation for steels, with an uncertainty of about 10 percent (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The geometry gives HB of about 415. The impression diameter of 3.0 mm lies in the 0.25 to 0.5 times the ball diameter window, so the test is valid and the estimated tensile strength is about 1430 MPa for a steel.
